name: Uma Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government, and your answers are confidential; what is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Uma, twenty-seven, and I lead a small line crew for the electric company. My two-year technical diploma helped me get here. I check the job plan, brief the crew, then climb or work from the bucket truck to repair lines; I like solving a fault, but weather and road closures wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what fills your day away from the poles?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing lights come back on while the crew is still packing up. I rent a place near the depot, have no children, and keep about eight months of expenses in savings; I run twice a week and call my sister on Sundays.

ans: I’d tell the crew that a little software won’t change the danger of a live line. My supervisor, Elena (my supervisor), can use it for schedules, but we still check the ground ourselves.
I don’t expect a big change to my pay or hours from this version. My savings are solid, though rent has risen twice this year and I notice it.
I’d keep leading the crew and try the scheduling tool Elena offers during a quiet week. I’d ask the safety officer to show us how it handles storm callouts before relying on it.
This feels manageable, with a small irritation about another screen to check. I’m glad the card leaves most work alone.
What would you check before trusting a new schedule?
I’d compare the software’s route with our map and the utility’s outage list. Last month a road closure made the printed route wrong, so I’d still ask the crew who knows that district.
say: I’d tell my crew **field judgment** still matters on a live line.
I’d say a schedule tool can help, but a storm plan needs a **human check**.
think: I expect **my pay** and hours to stay steady in this picture.
I still worry about **rising rent**, even without a major AI change.
do: Keep **leading the crew** on its current rotation.
Test the **scheduling tool** against our outage map before using it.
feel: I feel **steady**, with mild annoyance about another screen.

ans: I’d tell my crew that planning and paperwork may change before climbing does. Our outage notes and materials requests already take longer than they should.
I think the company could need fewer coordinators if AI handles schedules and reports. My own field role looks steadier for now, but promotions may narrow.
I’d learn the approved planning software this winter and ask Elena to let me test one district’s schedule. I’d also keep my rescue and switching certificates current.
I feel alert rather than frightened, because I have time and savings. Losing a path upward would still sting.

feel: I feel **watchful** because my role seems steadier than office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

ans: I’d tell the crew that full thinking AI in 2028 would hit planning before the poles. Robots around 2031 would make our field skills uncertain too.
I would expect the company to freeze hiring quickly if it could automate dispatch and inspections. I have savings, but I don’t want to assume a lead’s wage stays untouched.

Now I’d ask the training manager which electrical safety qualifications travel to building maintenance. In 2029, if AGI has arrived and my line hours fall, I’d apply to maintenance contractors while I still have this route.
Two years feels short, and the later robot date does not make my job safe. I’d sleep less while waiting to see what the company announces.

do: Ask the training manager about **transferable safety qualifications** now.

feel: I feel **anxious** about a short warning and uncertain field work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

ans: I’d tell my crew that five years is time to prepare, but not time to pretend nothing changes. AGI in 2031 would take our planning work before robots arrive around 2034.
I think I can move toward building maintenance while my electrical experience still counts. I’d be less worried than with a 2028 date, though the eventual robot work hangs over it.
I’d ask for a place on the company’s building systems course now and finish it before 2031. In 2032, after AGI arrives, I’d apply for maintenance work if line hours or pay had dropped.
Five years gives me room to act without panic. I still feel uneasy about whether maintenance will be hiring when many people move there.

I’d want a named qualification, a real employer asking for it and a course schedule I can manage around shifts. A vague promise of future work would not be enough.

ans: I’d tell the crew that ten years lets us plan carefully, while the 2039 robot date still changes the long view. I would not call outdoor work permanently protected.
I think I could build a second path before AGI arrives in 2036. I expect my income to hold for several years, but I’d worry about where the whole trade goes afterward.

I’d take a building systems course by 2029 and use the next years to get supervised experience. In 2037, if robots had not arrived yet, I’d keep working lines while taking paid maintenance shifts when available.
A decade makes me feel more in control, not carefree. I’d rather make a gradual change than leave a job I still like.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because two years is little time to shift a career. A clear employer-backed qualification and honest notice about staffing would help me plan without burning through savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d want people to remember that line work is physical but includes planning and permits too. I’m not asking for a promise that the work stays safe; I want enough warning to make a sensible move.

headlineQuote: I’d want people to remember that line work is physical but includes planning and permits too.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old lead** with a technical diploma and strong savings.
She enjoys restoring power but dislikes **weather**, road closures and lengthy permits.
She expects **field work** to change later than schedules and reports.
She responds to longer warnings with **training plans** and conditional applications.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to shift careers before thinking tasks change.
whatWouldHelp: An **employer-backed qualification** and honest staffing notice would let her plan without exhausting savings.
